def: Receive-side memory in a PCIe port where arriving TLPs wait until the port's internal consumer processes them. Partitioned by flow-control class (posted, non-posted, completion) and into header and data storage; its size is what the port advertises as credits.

A unit of receiver buffer space advertised to the transmitter: one header credit holds one TLP header, one data credit holds 16 bytes (4 DW) of payload. Kept separately for posted, non-posted and completion traffic per virtual channel (PH, PD, NPH, NPD, CplH, CplD).

An initial flow-control advertisement of zero for a credit type, meaning the receiver will always accept that type and the transmitter never gates on it. Commonly used for completions at requesters, which must then reserve buffer before issuing reads.

Time from a transmitter sending a TLP until it learns, through an UpdateFC DLLP, that the receiver has freed that TLP's buffer space. Includes serialization, flight, receiver drain time and UpdateFC scheduling. Credits needed for full rate = throughput × credit loop latency.

A PCIe feature introduced in Base Specification Revision 4.0 that adds HdrScale and DataScale fields to InitFC/UpdateFC DLLPs so credit values can be multiplied by a negotiated factor, allowing more credits outstanding on fast, wide links.

A transmitter has a TLP ready but cannot send it because a credit type it needs is exhausted. Comes in header, data and consumer-stall forms; a requester limited by its own completion buffer looks similar but involves no credit on the wire.

The PCIe procedure, used from 8 GT/s upward, in which the two ports of each lane adjust transmitter FIR settings (presets or coefficients) in Phases 0 to 3 so the receiver meets its error-rate target. Done per lane, per data rate and per direction.
Distortion in which the smeared energy of earlier or later bits lands on the current bit because the channel attenuates high frequencies. The main reason fast PCIe links need equalization.
An analog receiver stage that boosts high frequencies to compensate channel loss. Adapted inside the receiver; not negotiated on the link.
A receiver stage that subtracts the predicted tails of already-decided bits (post-cursor ISI). Cannot remove pre-cursor ISI, which is why transmitter preshoot exists.
Half the symbol rate: the highest fundamental frequency of the signal. Channel loss budgets are quoted at this frequency (for example 8 GHz for 16 GT/s NRZ, 16 GHz for 32 GT/s NRZ and 64 GT/s PAM4).
One of eleven defined PCIe transmitter settings, P0 to P10, each a target de-emphasis and preshoot for the 3-tap FIR. Used as starting points and common results of equalization from 8 GT/s upward.

A PCIe capability introduced in Revision 4.0 that lets software move a receiver's sampling point in time and voltage on a live link and count errors, measuring per-lane margin. It disturbs the receiver, so it is a caution-level operation.

An optional extended capability of root ports and switch downstream ports that, on configured uncorrectable errors, disables the link below the port, completes pending requests with UR or CA, and holds the link down until software clears DPC Trigger Status.

exp: Enhanced DPC (Root Port Extensions for DPC)
def: Common name for the root-port extensions to DPC that add RP PIO error logging and containment of failed CPU-originated requests, such as completion timeouts on MMIO reads.

A PCIe extended capability in switch ports, root ports and multi-function devices with controls (Source Validation, Translation Blocking, P2P Request/Completion Redirect, Upstream Forwarding, Egress Control, Direct Translated P2P) that force or block peer-to-peer routing. It determines IOMMU groups.
A full PCIe function that has an SR-IOV Extended Capability and creates and manages Virtual Functions. For an NVMe SSD, the primary controller sits behind the PF.

A lightweight PCIe function created by a PF's VF Enable, with its own Routing ID, BAR region (described by the PF's VF BARs) and MSI-X, but a reduced configuration space. Typically assigned directly to a virtual machine.

The NVMe controller associated with an SR-IOV Physical Function. It reports virtualization resources and executes Virtualization Management commands that assign flexible resources to secondary controllers and bring them online or offline.
An NVMe controller, typically associated with a Virtual Function, that depends on the primary controller for its flexible queue (VQ) and interrupt (VI) resources and its online/offline state.

A PCIe feature that treats the device and function fields of a Routing ID as a single 8-bit function number, allowing up to 256 functions on one device. Needed by most SR-IOV devices; the downstream port above must enable ARI Forwarding.

NVMe virtualization resource types: a VQ resource is controller capacity for one submission/completion queue pair, a VI resource for one interrupt vector. Private resources stay with the primary controller; flexible ones can be assigned to secondary controllers.

An NVMe 2.4 (2026) concept: a virtual SSD within a physical SSD that can be exposed to a VM and migrated live, using a configuration template identified by a 128-bit UUID. Field-level details are in the NVMe Base Specification 2.4.

A mandatory 512-byte NVMe log page with critical warnings, temperatures (Kelvin), available spare, percentage used, data units read/written (thousands of 512-byte units), command counts, power cycles, power-on hours, unsafe shutdowns, media errors and error log entry count.

NVMe log pages that carry vendor-specific diagnostic snapshots in a standardized container (header plus data areas). Collected for vendor root-cause analysis; capture before resetting a misbehaving drive.

An NVMe grouping of NVM sets and namespaces whose wear is managed together. The Endurance Group Information log (09h) reports its spare, percentage used, endurance estimate, data units and media units written.
